To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) sexual selection on cuticular hydrocarbon (CHC) phenotypes varies among geographic populations of D. serrata, and (2) the spatial pattern of variation is different in males and females.

(i) the strength and direction of sexual selection on cuticular hydrocarbon traits varies between populations, (ii) the variation in selection is not explained by neutral genetic structure or geographic distance, and (iii) variation in selection is associated with the presence or absence of the closely related species, Drosophila burchii.

(1) sexual selection is highly variable among populations, (2) variation in linear sexual gradients is associated with the presence/absence of a related species, (3) variation in linear and nonlinear sexual gradients is associated in females, (4) nonlinear sexual selection is more common in males than females, and (5) the strength and direction of linear and nonlinear sexual gradient variation are not necessarily correlated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of mate preference and the evolution of sexual dimorphism in Drosophia serrata.
the role of chance events in generating variation in multivariate sexual selection.
the spatial variation in sexual selection in D. serrata and how this may have been influenced by the presence of a closely related species, D. birchui, and by chance events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the fitness surfaces for male and female CHCs in D. serrata vary in a complex way across populations, with the variation in males driven by interspecific competition and that of females by chance events.

the variation in sexual selection among these populations is not consistent, but is likely to be influenced by the species’ ecology, the presence of other Drosophila species, the genetic structure of populations, and possibly other factors.
sexual selection on male and female CHCs is spatially and temporally variable and that the causes of such variation are likely to differ between males and females.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
variation in the fitness surface for CHCs in D. serrata is largely driven by variation in linear sexual and mutual sexual selection.
the spatial and temporal variation in the strength of sexual selection on CHC traits was greater than the variation in direction.
sexual selection in D. serrata males is more likely to be shaped by local adaptation, whereas in females it is shaped more by chance events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spatial and temporal variation in sexual selection is likely to be much greater than previously appreciated and may be an important source of phenotypic divergence between populations.
the multivariate fitness landscapes of sexual selection can vary dramatically among populations and that these differences are often not predicted by patterns of genetic differentiation.

the multivariate fitness landscapes that shape the evolutionary trajectories of populations can vary dramatically among populations and that the patterns of variation in these fitness surfaces are often consistent with the predictions of theoretical models.
